title: JESUS ASKED A MAN TO STRETCH OUT THE HAND HE COULDN’T USE. THE RELIGIOUS LEADERS RESPONDED BY PLANNING HIS DEATH.
paragraphs: JESUS ASKED A MAN TO STRETCH OUT THE HAND HE COULDN’T USE. THE RELIGIOUS LEADERS RESPONDED BY PLANNING HIS DEATH.
He walked into the synagogue carrying a hand that had withered. He walked out carrying a miracle. But while one man was being restored, other men were deciding that Jesus needed to die.
There is something almost unbearable about this story.
A man walks into a synagogue on the Sabbath with a hand he cannot properly use.
Luke gives us a detail Mark does not: it was his right hand that was withered (Luke 6:6).
We are not told his name.
We are not told how long he had lived this way.
We are not told whether he was born with it, injured later, or had watched his hand slowly become useless.
Scripture refuses to satisfy our curiosity.
Instead, it makes us stand in the room with him.
A synagogue.
A Sabbath.
Jesus.
A disabled man.
Religious leaders watching.
And underneath the sacred atmosphere...
a trap.
Mark tells us:
“And he entered again into the synagogue; and there was a man there which had a withered hand. And they watched him, whether he would heal him on the sabbath day; that they might accuse him.”
—Mark 3:1–2, KJV
Read that again.
They were watching Jesus.
But not because they wanted to believe.
Not because they were wondering whether the broken man might finally go home restored.
Not because compassion had awakened inside them.
They were watching for evidence.
They needed something they could use against Him.
Imagine being so committed to proving Jesus wrong that you can watch Him make a broken man whole and somehow make the miracle evidence against the Miracle Worker.
That is the scandal in this room.
And before we condemn them too quickly, we should ask a more uncomfortable question:
How many times have we wanted Jesus to behave according to our expectations instead of surrendering ourselves to His authority?
Because religious hardness rarely announces itself by saying, “I hate God.”
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it knows theology.
Sometimes it attends worship.
Sometimes it knows exactly what Christians are supposed to say.
Sometimes it can identify everyone else’s sin while carefully protecting its own.
Sometimes it would rather win an argument than see a wounded person restored.
And Jesus sees straight through it.
He tells the man:
“Stand forth.”
Come into the middle.
Imagine that moment.
The man could have remained hidden in the congregation.
His weakness could have stayed private.
But Jesus brings him where everyone can see him.
There are moments when Christ comforts us privately.
And there are moments when Christ calls us out of hiding.
Maybe that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because most of us have a “withered hand.”
Not necessarily something physically visible.
Maybe yours is the marriage nobody knows is collapsing.
The addiction you have learned to conceal.
The pornography history you keep deleting.
The resentment you call discernment.
The secret messages.
The affair nobody discovered.
The anger you unleash at home and hide at church.
The shame from something done to you.
The shame from something you did.
The prayer life that quietly disappeared.
The Bible that has remained closed while your phone remains open for hours.
The smile you wear in photographs while wondering privately how much longer you can keep pretending.
You know how to lift both hands during worship...
but there is still something inside you that feels withered.
And Jesus knows.
That is simultaneously terrifying and beautiful.
Because the One who sees what you hide is also the One who stepped toward the man everyone else was using as part of an argument.
Jesus looks at the religious leaders and asks a devastating question:
“Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill?”
—Mark 3:4, KJV
And nobody answers.
Silence.
Not because the question was complicated.
Because answering it honestly would expose them.

Matthew’s account adds another dimension. Jesus points out that if someone’s sheep fell into a pit on the Sabbath, that person would take hold of it and lift it out. Then He declares that a human being is worth far more than a sheep and concludes that doing good on the Sabbath is lawful (Matthew 12:11–12).
Jesus was not desecrating God’s Sabbath.
He was exposing what human hardness had done with it.
The Sabbath was God’s gift, not an excuse to become indifferent to suffering.
And Mark records something about Jesus here that should destroy the sentimental caricature of Christ as a permanently soft, harmless religious figure.
Jesus became angry.
The Greek text says:
μετ’ ὀργῆς — met’ orgēs
“With anger.”
But keep reading, because His anger is not petty rage.
Mark says He was:
συλλυπούμενος ἐπὶ τῇ πωρώσει τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν
Grieved over the hardness of their hearts.
Jesus is angry...
and grieving.
Why?
Because holy love does not look at hardened hearts with indifference.
Their problem was deeper than disagreement over Sabbath interpretation.
They had reached a place where a suffering man could stand directly in front of them and their primary concern was whether his healing could help them prosecute Jesus.
Think about that.
They could see the hand.
They could see the suffering.
Soon they would see the restoration.
But their hearts were becoming harder than the hand was withered.
Then Jesus turns toward the man.
And what He says almost sounds unreasonable.
Ἔκτεινον τὴν χεῖρά σου.
Ekteinon tēn cheira sou.
“Stretch out your hand.”
—Mark 3:5
Jesus commanded him to do the very thing his condition appeared to prevent him from doing.
Stretch it out.
The hand that does not work?
Stretch it out.
The part of you that has failed you?
Bring it toward Me.
The weakness you would rather hide?
Stop hiding it.
The thing everyone can see?
Stretch it out.
And here is where careless preaching can turn this beautiful passage into something Scripture never says.
The lesson is not that every physical disability will disappear immediately if a person simply has enough faith.
That is not what the text promises.
Christians must never weaponize this miracle against suffering people, as though an unhealed illness automatically proves deficient faith.
The point is that Jesus possesses authority the man does not possess.
The power is not in the man’s hand.
The power is in Christ.
The command comes from Jesus.
The restoration comes from Jesus.
The glory belongs to Jesus.
The man simply responds to the One speaking.
Mark says:
“And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.”
The impossible movement happened.
The hand opened.
Strength returned.
What had been withered was restored.
Can you imagine him looking at his own fingers?
Moving them.
Opening them.
Closing them.
Perhaps staring at a hand he had long ago stopped expecting to use normally again.
But while he is staring at his restored hand...
watch what happens next.
This is where the story becomes almost shocking.
Nobody throws a celebration.
Nobody among Jesus’ opponents falls to his knees.
Nobody says, “We were wrong.”
Nobody says, “Only God could do this.”
Mark writes:
καὶ ἐξελθόντες οἱ Φαρισαῖοι εὐθὺς μετὰ τῶν Ἡρῳδιανῶν συμβούλιον ἐδίδουν κατ’ αὐτοῦ ὅπως αὐτὸν ἀπολέσωσιν.
The Pharisees went out and immediately began taking counsel with the Herodians against Jesus concerning how they might destroy Him.
—Mark 3:6
That final Greek verb is chilling:
ἀπολέσωσιν — apolesōsin
To destroy.
To do away with.
The man stretches out his hand.
They go out to plan Jesus’ destruction.
A hand has just come alive...
and hardened hearts begin discussing death.
Do you see the horrifying irony?
Jesus had just asked them whether it was lawful on the Sabbath “to save life, or to kill.”
Then Jesus restores.
And they leave to plot His destruction.
Their actions answer the question their mouths refused to answer.
Jesus chooses restoration.
They choose destruction.
Jesus sees a suffering human being.
They see a theological problem.
Jesus restores what is withered.
Religion without mercy plots against the Restorer.
And this is why we cannot read this story merely as “Jesus versus those bad Pharisees.”
The Word must be allowed to turn toward us.
Because you can be close to Jesus physically, culturally, even religiously...
and still resist Him spiritually.
You can know Christian vocabulary and have a hardened heart.
You can defend biblical morality publicly while refusing to repent privately.
You can post Scripture and mistreat your spouse.
You can argue theology and neglect mercy.
You can sing about surrender while secretly negotiating which parts of your life Jesus is allowed to touch.
You can become so obsessed with appearing righteous that when Jesus exposes something withered inside you, your first instinct is not repentance...
but self-defense.
That is dangerous.
Because one of the most frightening spiritual conditions is not having something broken.
It is becoming comfortable keeping it broken when Jesus calls you into the light.
The man with the withered hand knew something was wrong.
The religious leaders apparently did not recognize how diseased their own hearts had become.
One man had an obvious disability.
Other men had an invisible hardness.
And strangely...
the man who entered visibly broken was the one who left restored.
Somebody reading this knows exactly why that sentence hurts.
You have spent years making sure nobody sees the withered place.
Maybe you learned how to function around it.
How to laugh around it.
How to minister around it.
How to work around it.
How to post around it.
How to worship around it.
You became so skilled at compensating for what was broken that almost nobody realizes how exhausted you are.
But Jesus does.
And He is not asking you to impress Him.
He is asking you to stop hiding from Him.
There is a difference.
The Gospel is not “fix yourself so Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel is that sinners who cannot rescue themselves are summoned to the Savior who can.
We have sinned against a holy God.
Not merely made mistakes.
Not merely accumulated trauma.
Not merely developed unhealthy habits.
We are sinners who need reconciliation with God.
And Jesus Christ did not come merely to make difficult lives more comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
The same Gospel of Mark that shows Jesus restoring this man’s hand moves relentlessly toward another scene.
Another day.
Another crowd.
Another confrontation.
Except eventually it is not the man with the withered hand being exposed before everyone.
It is Jesus.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Condemned.
Crucified.
The hands that restored the withered hand would themselves be stretched out.
Not because Rome ultimately overpowered Him.
Not because the Pharisees finally outsmarted Him.
Jesus willingly laid down His life.
The sinless Son of God bore sin’s judgment.
And what human beings intended for destruction became the place where God’s saving purpose was accomplished.
At the cross, our scandal meets His grace.
Our guilt meets His righteousness.
Our rebellion meets His mercy.
Our condemnation meets His sacrifice.
Our darkness meets the blood of the Lamb.
And death itself meets the risen Christ.
Jesus was crucified.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose again.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately a program of self-improvement.
It is news.
Good news.
The Savior has come.
The debt of sin can be forgiven.
The guilty can be justified.
The lost can be reconciled to God.
The ashamed can stop hiding.
The sinner can repent and come home.
Not because your record suddenly becomes impressive.
Because Christ’s finished work is sufficient.
Maybe you have spent years thinking, “If Jesus really knew what I did...”
He knows.
“If Jesus knew what I watch when nobody is around...”
He knows.
“If He knew what happened in that relationship...”
He knows.
“If He knew what I secretly think...”
He knows.
“If He knew how many times I promised to stop and went back...”
He knows.
“If He knew how cold my heart has become...”
He knows.
And the Gospel invitation is not to hide more effectively.
It is to repent and come to Christ.
Bring Him the withered place.
Bring Him the guilty place.
Bring Him the angry place.
Bring Him the sexually broken place.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the hypocrisy.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the version of you that never appears on Facebook.
Not because repentance earns salvation.
Because genuine faith turns toward the Savior and away from the sin that is destroying us.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace brings us to the One who breaks chains.
Maybe your prayer today does not need impressive language.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, my heart has become hard.”
“Jesus, I cannot heal myself.”
“Jesus, I believe. Help my unbelief.”
“Jesus, take what I have ruined and make my life Yours.”
And maybe your own version of Ἔκτεινον τὴν χεῖρά σου — “Stretch out your hand” begins there.
Not pretending.
Not performing.
Surrendering.
Not for performance.
Not because typing three words saves anybody.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending everything is fine.
Then read the other comments.
You may discover that the person sitting beside you in the digital “synagogue” has been carrying a withered place too.
Pray for somebody.
Encourage somebody.
Remind somebody that Jesus Christ is still worthy.
And please do not let this article die on your screen.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to suggest you know their secret.
You never know who has been scrolling silently while fighting a battle nobody around them can see.
Your share cannot save them.
But it can put the truth about the Savior in front of them.
And if sharing biblical truth helps another person hear about Christ, do not underestimate the value of that simple act.
Because eventually there may come a morning when you are the person who needs to read it again.
There may come a night when shame whispers that you should hide.
Come back and remember:
The man did not heal his own hand.
Jesus restored him.

We want this community to remain a place where Scripture is opened, Christ is exalted, sin is confronted, grace is proclaimed, wounded people are encouraged, believers are discipled, and nobody is told that religious performance can replace the Gospel.
Supporting Gospel-centered ministry is not a payment for God’s favor. Jesus Christ cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased. Salvation is God’s gift in Christ.

If God has used this ministry in your life and you want to help it reach another wounded person, another struggling marriage, another exhausted believer, another prodigal, another seeker, another person scrolling alone at two in the morning wondering whether Jesus could possibly want them...
Not because an algorithm is our savior.
Christ is.
It does not.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
It cannot.
Do it because truth is worth carrying.
Do it because somebody carried the Gospel to you.

Do it because there are people hiding wounds behind profile pictures, jokes, careers, church attendance, and carefully edited lives who desperately need to hear that Jesus Christ still calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Follow.
Save.
Share.
But above everything else...
come to Jesus.
Because eventually every secondary question in that synagogue disappears.
The argument disappears.
The trap disappears.
The watching crowd disappears.
And what remains is unforgettable:
A broken man.
A command from Christ.
A restored hand.
And religious men walking away from a miracle to discuss murder.
Do not become so accustomed to religion that you can stand near Jesus while resisting Jesus.
Do not become so committed to protecting your image that you refuse the Physician access to your wound.
Do not confuse knowing Christian things with knowing Christ.
Do not spend your life hiding the very thing you need to surrender.
The man stretched out what was withered.
The religious leaders protected what was hardened.
One left restored.
The others walked deeper into darkness.
So now the story turns toward you.
What are you going to do when Jesus confronts the place you have spent years hiding?
Run?
Defend it?
Explain it?
Blame someone?
Protect your reputation?
Or finally bring it into the light?
Maybe today your confession is simply:
“No more hiding.”
And perhaps somebody reading your words will find enough courage to stop hiding too.
Because the most unforgettable part of this story may not be that Jesus told a man to stretch out a hand he could not use.
It may be that the man trusted Jesus enough to stop hiding what was broken...
while the people convinced they could already see clearly walked away plotting against the only One who could save them.
Never be so afraid of exposing what is withered that you protect it from the hands of the One who was wounded to redeem you.
